newsitem.title: USA: Gingrich asks Greenspan to help Congress raise GDP.
newsitem.headline: Gingrich asks Greenspan to help Congress raise GDP.

text.p: House Speaker Newt Gingrich said on Friday he had asked Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan to help Congress devise policies to improve the real rate of U.S. economic growth.

Speaking at a news conference in his district office, the Georgia Republican said he wanted Congress' Joint Economic Committee to develop a series of hearings and to propose a way of maximizing the growth of America's gross domestic product.
Gingrich spoke to Greenspan by telephone after telling business leaders early on Friday that he would hope to boost U.S. economic growth to between 4 percent and 5 percent a year.
"I was asking Alan if he would be willing to help us intellectually look at the model of what would maximize growth in the United States," the speaker said.
Gingrich disclosed little about Greenspan's reaction but said the Fed chairman was "deeply committed" to the highest possible real growth rate.

Gingrich emphasised that his discussion with Greenspan was not an attempt to get the central bank to be more open about economic growth following last week's 25 basis-point hike in U.S. interest rates.

"He made the point that we shouldn't get too locked into a specific number because the truth is the numbers are not very accurate, given the size of our economy and the complexity of it," Gingrich said.

After fielding repeated questions from reporters on the subject, Gingrich sought to play down the formality of his discussion with Greenspan. "He's an economist, I'm a historian. We talk about ideas, five or six times a year," he said.

Earlier on Friday, in his first public appearance since returning from a 10-day tour of Asia, the Georgia Republican advocated a heady mix of tax cuts, reform and deregulation as the means for making the U.S. economy emulate the vitality of Taiwan, South Korea and China.
"It is unconscionable to have the Federal Reserve system close off economic growth because of some theoretical model," Gingrich said.
"Our goal should be to say bluntly, up front: we want a high growth, high income, high take-home pay, high opportunity society," he said. "And we're not going to settle for anything less."

Speaking weeks after he was widely criticised in his own party for suggesting that Congress could make lower taxes a secondary priority, Gingrich called for getting rid of taxes on savings and investments as an incentive to job growth.
He also vowed lawmakers would seek to completely overhaul the Internal Revenue Service if not scrap the federal tax agency altogether.

"You want Chinese or Hong Kong or Taiwanese growth rates? You've got to have a tax system that favours economic growth. If you want more jobs and you want more wealth and you want a better future ... there should be no taxes on savings and investments," he said.

"We believe the Constitution should be amended to require a super-majority to raise taxes, to protect the taxpayer from a political structure that is too willing to use your money to pay off their political cronies," he said.
